This section outlines how we value carbon sequestration as an ecosystem service within the GEP framework. The analysis focuses specifically on carbon sequestration provided by terrestrial ecosystems, which is appraised in terms of its contribution to climate change mitigation. By quantifying the carbon sequestration capacity of these ecosystems, we aim to capture their role in reducing atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations, thereby contributing to global climate regulation.



# Methods


## Estimating Quantity


We followed the methodology outlined in @johnson2023investing to quantify global carbon sequestration. To estimate the quantity of carbon sequestered, we implemented a two-stage modeling framework, as illustrated in panels (a) and (b) of @fig-carbon-workflow.

First, we utilized an advanced global carbon density map developed by @spawn2020harmonized to update the carbon pool. This dataset consists of harmonized vegetation-specific maps that integrate both aboveground and belowground biomass into a single, comprehensive spatial representation for the year 2010, thereby enabling more accurate assessments of carbon stocks across diverse ecosystems. To construct the carbon pool table or carbon density lookup table, we combined the 300 m land use and land cover (LULC) data from the European Space Agency Climate Change Initiative Land Cover (ESA CCI LC) with the carbon zone map employed by @gibbs2008new. This integrated methodology enhances both the spatial resolution and contextual relevance of carbon stock estimations.

Second, we applied the updated carbon density lookup table and the carbon zone map to a time series of LULC data, also derived from ESA CCI LC, to enable dynamic assessments of carbon storage over time.

![Workflow for quantifying and valuing global carbon storage. (a) The Data Preparation phase integrates the carbon zone map employed by @gibbs2008new, base-year ESA LULC data, and carbon density data from @spawn2020harmonized to generate a carbon density lookup table. (b) The Application phase applies the lookup table to the base-year LULC and carbon zone maps to obtain per-cell carbon density, then multiplies by cell area to obtain per-cell carbon stocks. The same calculation applies to any LULC time series for dynamic assessment. (c) The Valuation phase sums carbon stocks per country and multiplies by the annual rental social cost of carbon to yield GEP by country.](figures/GEP_carbon_workflow.png){#fig-carbon-workflow width=100%}


## Estimating Price

To estimate the value of carbon sequestration, we employed the rental social cost of carbon (SCC) [@parisa_time_2022] as the pricing metric. @parisa_time_2022 provides the theoretical rationale for quantifying the value of short-term carbon storage, which corresponds to carbon sequestration. Following this approach, and within the framework of Gross Ecosystem Product (GEP), we estimate the annual value of carbon sequestration as follows:

$$
\text{Carbon Rental Rate} = P_C(t) - P_C(t+1)e^{-r} = P_C(t)\left(1 - e^{-r} \right)
$$


where $P_C(t)$ denotes the social cost of carbon in year $t$, and $r$ represents the net discount rate equal to
the difference between the discount rate and the rate of growth of carbon prices. This formulation reflects the rental valuation approach, capturing the annualized benefit of temporarily storing one metric ton of CO2 for one year. This measure represents the annualized marginal damage cost of emitting an additional metric ton of CO2, thereby aligning our valuation approach with established climate policy frameworks and principles of intertemporal cost-benefit analysis. We adopt a carbon price of \$678.33 per metric ton of carbon (C), corresponding to the mean social cost of CO2 of roughly \$185 per metric ton of CO2 estimated by @rennert_comprehensive_2022 (converted to a per-carbon basis by the 44/12 mass ratio). This value is employed for $P_C(t)$, the carbon price at time $t$, and a discount rate of 2% is applied, following the same source. The rental rate the model applies is read year by year from the carbon-price series (`rental scc r2%` in `carbon_prices.xlsx`). For the base year 2019 it is \$13.19 per ton of C. The series takes the \$185 per ton of CO2 for 2020 back to 2019 by US inflation, \$181.60 per ton of CO2 or \$665.87 per ton of C, and applies $1 - e^{-0.02}$ to it. The same rate on the 2020 value, \$678.33, gives \$13.43.

## Valuation

After estimating both the quantity and price of carbon sequestration, the economic value of carbon sequestration, is calculated as:

$$
\text{GEP}_{\text{carbon storage and sequestration}} = Q \cdot P \cdot \lambda = \text{Carbon Storage} \times \text{Rental SCC} \times 1
$$

where $Q$ represents the quantity of carbon storage (in metric tons), and $P$ denotes the annual rental SCC per ton. This formulation aligns with the GEP framework, translating biophysical carbon sequestration into monetary value.


## Source and implementation

The write-up is the authors' terrestrial carbon document of 28 October 2026 in the shared folder
of current write-ups. The registered code is the `terrestrial_carbon` folder of
`NatCapTEEMs/global_invest_dev` at `3be9ae5` (folder last changed at `f0de419`). The library
follows its chain: Spawn et al. (2020) above- and below-ground biomass carbon for 2010, scaled
from integers to Mg C per hectare and added, reprojected by nearest neighbour onto the land-cover
grid, a lookup of the mean density per land-cover class and carbon zone, the 2019 density raster
from it, times hectares per cell, summed by region and then by country. The lookup's classes come
from the 2010 land cover, the year of the Spawn map, as in the write-up and the authors' current
code, and the lookup is applied to the 2019 land cover.

Carbon zone 0 is the zone map's fill, the cells outside every carbon zone. As in the authors' code,
it has no key in the lookup, so its cells carry no density, missing rather than zero. A country
whose regions hold no valid cell is therefore missing, a blank row. A country whose valid cells sum
to zero is zero. The price is the series value at full precision, 13.185088586933462 per Mg C. The
authors' table rounds it to 13.19, which on the same stock puts their total \$1.98 billion higher.

The library differs from the registered code in three places, none of them a method change. It
publishes one row per country, where the registered code repeats a split country's value on
each of its sub-regions (six countries, 23.49% too high in total). It gives each cell to the one
region that covers its centre, where the registered code lets a border cell count in both
neighbours. And it runs end to end, where the registered reprojection step reads a path nothing
sets.

## Output

`gep_calculation` writes `gep_by_country_base_year.csv` into its own task directory, holding the
r250 identifiers and attributes, `year`, `terrestrial_carbon_quantity` (Mg C), the rental rate
`rental scc r2%` and `terrestrial_carbon_gep`.

## Coverage

The published table is one row for each of the account's 250 countries, base year 2019, in 2019
USD. 234 rows carry a value, totalling \$5,328,155,728,197.37 on 404.1 billion Mg C. Antarctica is
zero and 15 small islands and territories are missing, the same rows as in the authors' table. A zero means the
computation returned zero. A missing row means the data to compute one is absent.

## What is open

- The residual against the authors' 1 September table is explained in total, not country by
  country. Keys and masks are identical. Priced at their 13.19, the values differ by \$6,659 in
  total, 504.86 Mg C or 1.25e-9 of the stock, and every country lies within the bound that float32
  storage of the densities allows, the largest at 9.1e-8. In total the residual splits into the
  lookup means and the per-cell storage. The account keeps 13.185088586933462 from the price
  table, where the authors' code uses 13.19.
- The lookup means are checked for range and plausibility, not recomputed from the Spawn raster,
  which takes one global pass over 8.4 billion cells.
